title: Why GPS needs relativity
subtitle: Clocks in orbit gain 38.6 microseconds a day, and how GPS cancels it

scenes.title: Do two perfect clocks agree?
scenes.narration: Here is a question that sounds too simple.

steps.say: Put a perfect clock on a satellite, and another on the ground. Do they keep the same time?
Most people say yes. They don’t, and if nobody fixed it, your map would be useless within a day.

scenes.title: A ring of clocks, 20,200 km up
scenes.narration: Start with your phone, sitting on the ground.

steps.say: Your phone has no idea where it is. It has to be told.
Twenty thousand kilometres up, a ring of satellites circles the planet. The drawing is to scale.
Each one moves at almost four kilometres a second, and goes all the way round in just under twelve hours.
Every satellite carries an atomic clock, and keeps sending out the time.
The signal takes about a fifteenth of a second to reach you.

scenes.title: How a phone finds itself
scenes.narration: Your phone compares the time in each signal with when it arrived.

steps.say: The gap, times the speed of light, is how far away that satellite is. That puts you somewhere on a circle around it.
A second and a third circle cross at just one point.
That point is you. Out in three dimensions, a fourth satellite also corrects the cheap clock in your phone.
Now make one satellite’s clock a millionth of a second late.
Light goes three hundred metres in that time, so that circle lands three hundred metres off, and the crossing point moves.

scenes.title: Gravity gains more than speed loses
scenes.narration: So the satellite clocks must agree with the ground to within billionths of a second.

steps.say: And Einstein says they can’t, for two reasons that pull opposite ways.
Clocks run faster where gravity is weaker. Twenty thousand kilometres up, that makes the satellite clock gain about forty six microseconds a day.
Moving clocks run slower. At almost four kilometres a second, that costs it about seven microseconds a day.
Gravity wins. Together, the clock in orbit runs ahead by 38.6 microseconds every day.

scenes.title: Higher orbits gain, low ones lose
scenes.narration: Which effect wins depends on how high the orbit is.

steps.say: Here is how much a clock gains each day against the ground, for an orbit of any size.
Close to the Earth, low orbits are fast, so speed wins. A clock on the space station loses about 24 microseconds a day.
At about nine and a half thousand kilometres from the centre, the two effects cancel exactly.
GPS orbits much higher, so gravity wins, by thirty eight point six.
Further out the curve flattens, as both effects fade.

scenes.title: Eleven kilometres off, every day
scenes.narration: Thirty eight microseconds sounds like nothing.

steps.say: But light goes 11.6 kilometres in that time. Every distance your phone measures would grow wrong by that much each day.
After a week, it is 81 kilometres. The map would put you in the next town, then the next country.

scenes.title: Set it slow before launch
scenes.narration: So the engineers do something strange. They make the satellite clocks wrong on purpose.

steps.say: Tuned like the ground clock, the satellite clock creeps ahead, a little more every day.
So before launch, it is tuned a hair slow: four parts in ten billion.
Up in orbit, relativity speeds it up by exactly that much, and seen from the ground it ticks in step.

scenes.title: Every clock in step, and you found
scenes.narration: Every satellite in the ring carries the same slow tuned clock.

steps.say: Seen from the ground, they all tick in step.
Orbits are not perfect circles, so your phone adds one last small correction, up to about twenty three billionths of a second.
Relativity is not just a theory here. It is in your pocket.
